items.t: TSMC reportedly weighs 3D DRAM production at Nvidia’s request
sum: The chipmaker's early-stage memory plans point to a long-term bet, not a quick fix for the AI-driven shortage

TSMC has reportedly begun internal planning to manufacture advanced 3D DRAM memory chips at the request of Nvidia, one of its biggest customers. For a company that has historically stayed out of the memory business, that is a notable change of direction.
The catch: anyone hoping this ends the current memory crunch soon may need to wait. The effort is still in its early stages, with no firm capital commitments and no production timeline attached.
The reports surfaced on November 6, 2026. They describe TSMC exploring how it might produce 3D DRAM, a type of memory that builds upward rather than spreading out across a flat surface.
The project is reportedly being led by Hsu Kuo-chin, TSMC’s vice president of Advanced Packaging. His team is said to be weighing several paths forward.
Those options reportedly include building new fabrication facilities or adapting existing ones. Neither choice has been locked in.
The backdrop is a severe memory shortage driven by AI demand. That shortage is expected to weigh on both supply and pricing well into 2028.

Taiwan Stocks Plunge Record 3,737 Points Intraday; TSMC Hits Limit-Down at NT$2,020, Wiping NT$5.7 Trillion in Market Value
sum: Taiwan stocks opened on Friday (the 6th) to devastating selling pressure. The Taiwan Weighted Index gapped open at 38,915.76 points before plunging in a straight line, touching an intraday low of 37,837.05 points—a collapse of 3,737.67 points, or nearly 9%—setting a record for the largest single-day intraday point drop in history. Market heavyweight Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (2330.TW) opened straight to its limit-down price of NT$2,020, a single-day plunge of NT$220, instantly wiping out roughly NT$5.7 trillion (approximately $172.8 billion) in market value and marking the largest intraday point drop on record. The number of limit-down stocks on the main board at one point exceeded 240, with electronics heavyweights and high-priced "thousand-dollar" stocks collapsing across the board as panic rapidly intensified.

The epicenter of this historic crash was the U.S. stock market. After the U.S. Midterm Elections handed Democrats control of both the Senate and the House, investors grew worried about tighter future regulation of artificial intelligence (AI) and possible restrictions on data center construction. Combined with the massive capital expenditures of large technology companies, the market began reassessing the growth prospects of AI infrastructure investment. All four major U.S. indices tumbled on the 5th: the Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged 1,833.06 points, or 3.44%, to close at 51,523.06; the S&P 500 fell 334.89 points, or 4.36%, to 7,353.73; and the Nasdaq Composite plummeted 1,421.51 points, or 5.52%, to 24,315.00—its largest single-day decline in 19 months—and has fallen more than 10% from its October record high, officially entering correction territory.

The semiconductor sector bore the brunt of the selloff. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 1,257.52 points, or 12.25%, to close at 9,011.14. TSMC's ADR tumbled 10.78% to $353.10 (approximately NT$12,000). AI chip leader Nvidia fell 9.26%, AMD plunged 17.26%, Broadcom dropped 10.43%, Intel fell 10.33%, and memory stock Micron sank 17.46%. According to Reuters, the market value of S&P 500 constituents evaporated by roughly $3 trillion (approximately NT$98.9 trillion) in a single day, showing that the correction has spread from semiconductors to the broader technology sector.

Philadelphia Semiconductor Index Plunge Drags Taiwan Stocks Down Over 900 Points in Early Trading; TSMC Turns Negative, Falls NT$15
sum: Although the U.S. Dow Jones Industrial Average surged more than 1,500 points after midterm election results became clear, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index—the gauge most closely correlated with Taiwan stocks—bucked the trend with a 3.13% plunge, dragging Taipei stocks down as much as 905.91 points in early trading today (the 5th), with the Taiwan Weighted Index touching a low of 42,043. Foundry leader Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (2330.TW) turned negative from positive, falling NT$15 to NT$2,245.

Reviewing U.S. stock performance on the 4th, the Dow Jones Industrial Average surged 1,569.40 points, or 3.03%, to close at 53,356.12—its largest single-day gain since April 9, 2025. The S&P 500 rose 119.70 points, or 1.58%, to 7,688.62, while the Nasdaq gained 364.51 points, or 1.44%, to 25,736.52. Market participants interpreted the Democrats' landslide midterm victory as a positive: investors bet that a White House and Congress checking each other would benefit corporate operations. Combined with expectations that the Iran war could end earlier than expected and a sharp drop in oil prices, buying sentiment was further ignited.

However, semiconductor stocks did not join the celebration. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 331.74 points, or 3.13%, to 10,268.66, retreating to a six-month low. AI chip leader Nvidia dropped 3.17%, while TSMC's ADR weakened 2.24% to $395.75, representing a premium of about 15% over its Taipei-traded shares. Micron tumbled 7%, and Super Micro Computer also sank 5.7%—even with strong quarterly earnings, they could not overcome market concerns that AI infrastructure investment may slow. AMD bucked the trend with a 1% gain to $488.78, buoyed by rising demand for AI graphics processors and better-than-expected earnings.

Taiwan stocks had just fallen 358.63 points, or 0.83%, on the 4th to close at 42,948.91, with trading value of approximately NT$1.1769 trillion (approximately $35.9 billion). The index hit an intraday high of 43,741.54 and a low of 41,855.82, showing sharp volatility. Taiwan Index Futures in the night session bucked the trend to close up 201 points at 43,404, a gain of 0.5%, diverging from the spot market.

Kopsi, Taiwan, other Asian stocks tumble after US midterm elections signal Democratic victory. What’s the
sum: Technology-heavy markets bore the brunt of the sell-off, with South Korea's KOSPI dropping 4% and Taiwan's benchmark index falling more than 3% to its lowest level since late July. The weakness also pulled MSCI's emerging markets index down 1.8%, taking it close to a seven-month low.

The US midterm election results could influence several major market themes, including the expansion of AI data centres, the country's fiscal outlook, defence expenditure and regulatory policies covering sectors such as healthcare, banking and cryptocurrencies.
South Korean chipmakers came under heavy selling pressure, with SK Hynix declining 6.1% and Samsung Electronics falling 4.1%. Taiwan's TSMC lost 2.2%.

Emerging Asian currencies, meanwhile, strengthened broadly as the US dollar weakened sharply. The South Korean won led the gains, rising 0.5%, while the Malaysian ringgit and Philippine peso each edged up around 0.1%.

US bond yields fell on Tuesday as investors sought the safety of government debt amid a sharp decline in equity futures, following projections of substantial Democratic wins in the 2026 US midterm elections. The dollar weakened against major currencies following the developments. The euro gained 0.5% to $1.1249, while the pound rose 0.37% to $1.3464. The dollar index fell 0.37% to 101.34.

Investors remain on edge that a substantial Democratic majority in the Senate, in a scenario being described as a potential 'blue wave', could weigh on AI-related stocks. The sector has already retreated in recent weeks amid questions about the pace of data centre spending. However, with votes still being counted in several states, investors cautioned that the market reaction could be temporary, given the sharp swings often seen during election nights.

Election projections pointed to Democrats securing control of both chambers of Congress. Poll estimates indicated a Democratic victory in the House, while the Senate contest was initially still uncertain.

Cathie Wood Just Sold $24.6 Million of Surging Chip Stock
sum: Last week, Cathie Wood's ARK Invest sold about 56,000 shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (NYSE:TSM), known as TSMC, in a trade valued at roughly $24.6 million.
The numbers imply a price of about $440 per share, based on rounded figures.
TSMC stock has climbed more than 75% since ARK's previous round of buying in July 2026. The latest sale stands in contrast to that period, when ARK was buying the stock.
In simple terms, $100 of TSMC stock bought then would now be worth more than $175.

The sale is likely aimed at locking in profit, or selling shares after a rise to secure the gain. The move follows large gains across the semiconductor sector, which covers companies that make computer chips.

The trade is part of a portfolio rotation, a shift of money out of some holdings and into others. Wood appears to be using the proceeds from semiconductor trimming, meaning partial sales, to fund new bets.

sum: - TSMC shares fell approximately 16.4% from their monthly peak of $485.80
- TSMC reported a 68.7% increase in quarterly net profit and raised its revenue forecast
- TSMC's October revenue figures, scheduled for Nov. 10, could provide more insight into semiconductor demand

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) experienced a sharp reversal in October 2026 when its stock fell approximately 16.4% from its monthly closing high despite reporting record quarterly earnings and raising its revenue forecast. The decline came as concerns over artificial intelligence spending and semiconductor valuations weighed on technology stocks.
TSMC shares closed Oct. 30 at $406.13, down 5.95% for the day and approximately 16% for the month. The stock reached a closing high of $485.80 on Oct. 5.

TSMC started October with strong momentum, and climbed from $459.20 on Oct. 1 to $485.80 by Oct. 5. However, the rally quickly lost steam as investors began reassessing the valuations of semiconductor companies benefiting from the AI boom.
By Oct. 14, TSMC stock retreated to $430, before declining even more to $412.61 on Oct. 16.

Cathie Wood Shifts From AI Chips to Robinhood and Air Taxis in Latest ARK Trades
sum: Cathie Wood just pulled millions out of two of this year's hottest AI chip winners and poured it into a battered broker and a pair of air taxi startups burning through cash. The trades raise a pointed question: does ARK…

Cathie Wood’s ARK Invest spent Wednesday taking money out of two of 2026’s best AI chip stocks and putting it into a beaten-down broker and two air taxi developers. According to Benzinga, ARK bought about $9.1 million of Robinhood (NASDAQ:HOOD | HOOD Price Prediction) on October 28, 2026. Benzinga also reported purchases of about $4.2 million of Archer Aviation (NYSE:ACHR) and about $3.3 million of Joby Aviation (NYSE:JOBY). On the same day, Benzinga said ARK sold about $3.3 million of AMD (NASDAQ:AMD) and about $4.7 million of Taiwan Semiconductor (NYSE:TSM). ARK kept adding to the air taxi names on consecutive days. These are reported fund trades. Wood has not publicly explained them.

AMD is up 139.65% year to date at $513.24, even after falling 9.39% today as Intel’s earnings report raised concerns. AMD’s results give no sign of a slowdown. Second-quarter revenue rose 50.1% to $11.54B, data center sales jumped 107% to $6.72B, and management guided third-quarter revenue to about $13B. CEO Lisa Su said, “We are still in the early stages of a multiyear AI adoption cycle.”

TSMC makes the chips for AMD and most other AI designers. Its stock is up 36.23% this year. Third-quarter revenue reached $46.72B with a 66.4% gross margin, and the company expects about 44% full-year revenue growth. CEO C.C. Wei said, “We did not see any sign of a slowdown.” The sales are tiny next to market caps of $836.84B and $2.13T. They read as ARK shifting money from proven winners toward ideas the market has marked down.

Robinhood runs a trading app that has grown into banking, credit cards, crypto, and prediction markets. Its shares fell after its latest quarterly results as a crypto slump weighed on profits. The stock trades at $84.24, down 8.03% today and 27.52% over the past month.

Robinhood’s second-quarter filing shows the mix shifting. Revenue from event contracts grew more than tenfold to $156M while crypto revenue fell 38% to $100M. Platform assets reached $369B. ARK was already the largest holder among the funds tracked, with 5,236,031 shares as of June 30.

AI Earnings Shock: Taiwan Stocks Plunge More Than 1,400 Points Intraday, TSMC Falls Below NT$2,400
sum: AI Earnings Spark Monetization Doubts as Taiwan Stocks Plunge Over 1,600 Points Intraday, TSMC Falls Below NT$2,400

Earnings from U.S. tech giants have repeatedly stoked doubts about AI monetization, and Taiwan stocks opened lower on the 30th before selling pressure spread rapidly. The Taiwan Weighted Index fell to an intraday low of 44,726.26, plunging more than 1,642 points at one stage and breaking below both the 45,000-point mark and its half-year line around 45,280, marking one of the sharpest single-day declines in recent memory. The index ended at 45,211.83, down 1,156.50 points, or 2.49%, with turnover expanding to NT$879.257 billion (approximately $27.0 billion).

The epicenter of the selloff came from across the Pacific. After Google parent Alphabet reported earnings, markets grew concerned about its AI-related capital expenditures and cash flow position, sending its shares down 12.64% in a single day and wiping roughly $500 billion off its market value in one stroke. Amazon and Intel then reported after the U.S. close with results that likewise fell short of expectations; Intel's fourth-quarter outlook came in far below estimates, sending its shares down more than 21% after hours and unleashing a wave of disappointed selling across Asian trading on the 30th.

Heavyweight stocks bore the brunt. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (2330.TW) fell NT$45 to NT$2,370, down 1.86%, surrendering the NT$2,400 level; MediaTek (2454.TW) dropped nearly 5%; Delta Electronics (2308.TW) and AUO (2409.TW) both hit limit-down; Yageo (2327.TW) tumbled 7.55%; United Microelectronics (2303.TW) fell more than 3%; and Nanya Technology (2408.TW) lost 4.72%. High-priced stocks were also hammered, with market leader Aspeed Technology (5274.TW) down nearly 7% and runner-up King Slide Works (2059.TW) extending losses after falling below NT$10,000, leaving just 46 stocks trading above NT$1,000 intraday.

Not everything was in the red. Shipping and telecom names became safe havens, with Evergreen Marine (2603.TW) closing at NT$271.5, up NT$10.50 or 4.02%; Wan Hai Lines (2615.TW) closing at NT$120, up 4.35%; Chunghwa Telecom (2412.TW) rising 1.27% to NT$160 after touching a matching record high intraday; and Far EasTone Telecommunications (4904.TW) closing at NT$114, up 0.88%.

SpaceX’s Stock Price Drops After Q3 2026 Earnings
sum: Space Exploration Technologies Corp's (ticker: SPCX) second public quarterly earnings release on the 20th of October – marking nine months (9M) of its Fiscal Year (FY) 2026 – prompted a 7% price rise the next day. Since the 20th till the 27th (a full week later), the stock has given up those gains and is running flat.
The results were heralded as holding a number of positives but, upon consideration of all the facts, the lukewarm reaction might be merited.
As of 9M 2026, revenues for the full year are trending to be 40% lower than the previous FY.

2025 was the year net income was flat at near-zero despite total costs and expenses showing a massive spike while operating income ran deeply negative. As of 9M 2026, operating income is running positive at $705 million and net income is a loss at over a billion.

The single most encouraging line item was revenue from "Super Intelligence" (SI), a term that was announced by President Trump as a replacement for "Artificial Intelligence" and subsequently adopted by SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. AI-related income has become a major contributor to top-line revenues.
AI-driven revenue went to a solid $7.56 billion in Q3 2026 versus $813 million a year ago. In the quarter, SpaceX also closed its $60 billion purchase of AI coding startup Cursor.

Within "SI", AI-driven advertising – made available by the likes of X, once known as "Twitter" and now owned by Musk – was a minor contributor to revenue. A substantial portion of "SI" revenue was accrued from renting capacity to other AI rivals such as Google and Anthropic (as shown in "SI Solutions & Infrastructure" segment).

items.t: TSMC's Credit Upgrade Lands as AI Funding Fears Weigh on the Stock
sum: Moody's Ratings lifted TSMC's credit rating from Aa3 to Aa2, with the outlook shifting from positive to stable, according to media reports on Wednesday. The upgrade rests on the chipmaker's lead in advanced semiconductors, its balance sheet strength and demand for AI chips — a verdict on credit quality that says nothing about whether the equity is cheap.

That distinction matters on a day when the stock is under pressure. TSMC shares fell 4.2% as a global selloff in technology and AI names gathered pace, with worries about how the AI buildout will be financed and rising oil prices weighing on risk appetite. Reuters tied the weakness in Asian tech to concerns over the cost of AI investments and mounting tensions in the Gulf, while the Associated Press pointed to anxiety over borrowing costs for data centres and AI chips. The decline reflects a sector-wide repricing of risk, not a fresh set of numbers from the company.

The operating backdrop for Moody's decision came roughly a week ago, when TSMC reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of NT$1,494.24 billion, up 50.9% year on year. Net profit for the same period reached NT$763.06 billion, with diluted earnings per share climbing 68.7%.

TSMC also raised its full-year 2026 forecast for revenue growth in US dollar terms to 44% about a week ago — a company projection, not a delivered annual result. The AI chip demand that Moody's highlighted rounds out the picture, showing the rating decision does not rest on past profit alone.

Analyst sentiment has been supportive too. Gil Luria of DA Davidson reaffirmed his buy rating and $500 price target on 16 October, though that call predates the current selloff and is not a response to it.

Alongside the brighter credit assessment, TSMC is dealing with the aftermath of a serious accident. Four workers employed by a contractor died on Tuesday after a fall at the Fab 22 construction site in Kaohsiung; the cause is under investigation. On Wednesday the company said it had voluntarily suspended steel structure work at its construction sites across Taiwan, a measure that extends well beyond the immediate location. The halt covers steel erection only and should not be confused with a standstill in chip production.

SpaceX Surges Over 12% Intraday, Market Cap Briefly Tops TSMC; Chinese ADRs Slide Broadly
sum: During the U.S. trading session on October 21, SpaceX shares surged more than 12% intraday, pushing its total market value to $2.25 trillion and briefly overtaking TSMC, making it the day's most closely watched focus. At the same time, popular Chinese ADRs weakened collectively, with the Nasdaq Golden Dragon China Index falling more than 3% intraday—a sharp contrast to the broad gains among large-cap tech stocks.

SpaceX shares hit an intraday high of $165.641, the biggest single-day gain since August, and were still up more than 9% as of press time. On the news front, the company's third-quarter revenue reached $14.6 billion, up 161% year-over-year. Elon Musk said that, based on current trends, annual recurring revenue (ARR) could reach $500 billion to $1 trillion by the end of 2027. That guidance significantly exceeded market expectations and was the direct trigger for the stock's sharp rally.

Space-concept stocks rose broadly in response. Rocket Lab gained 2.79%, Planet Labs 3.21%, AST SpaceMobile 1.54% and Intuitive Machines 3.70%. The semiconductor sector also advanced mostly, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index up more than 1%; memory-chip names Seagate Technology and Western Digital rose more than 2%, and South Korea's SK Hynix gained more than 1%. Optical communications names were active: Lumentum rose 5.97%, Coherent 4.24%, Applied Optoelectronics 4.69%, Ciena 5.46% and Marvell Technology 3.27%.

AI server makers emerged as another main thread. Super Micro Computer shares rose 12%, the biggest gain in two months. The company preliminarily estimated first-quarter net sales at $18.5 billion to $19.5 billion, far above market expectations; it also announced a partnership with Nokia to deploy Nvidia's Aerial RAN computing solution at the network edge to support low-latency AI services. Dell Technologies rose more than 7% and Hewlett Packard Enterprise more than 4%.

Large-cap tech stocks were mixed. Tesla rose more than 3%, Meta and Nvidia more than 2%, and Apple 0.46%; Google fell more than 2%, Amazon more than 1%, and Microsoft edged lower. Netflix dropped more than 6% to a more than two-year low; the company expects fourth-quarter revenue of about $13.44 billion, below analysts' estimate of $13.51 billion.

ASML, TSMC Report This Week: What Traders Are Watching After A 6-Day Chip Stock Slide
sum: - Results from ASML and TSMC would offer key signals for future chip demand.
- Retail sentiment toward ASML strengthened, while TSMC sentiment has cooled as both stocks face pressure from the broader chip selloff.

ASML Holding NV (ASML) and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSM) are poised to offer crucial clues about the health of the AI trade with their quarterly reports this week as a broad selloff in chip stocks raises the stakes.

Semiconductor stocks have been pressured; the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) fell for a sixth straight session on Tuesday, as fresh investor doubts about whether massive spending on AI infrastructure will generate sufficient returns, along with rising bond yields and financing costs, add to concerns.

Recent comments from Broadcom CEO Hock Tan about possible capital constraints in the AI buildout have added to the unease, while reports of Chinese memory-maker CXMT narrowing the technology gap have pressured memory stocks.

ASML's results matter because demand for advanced chipmaking equipment can signal future chip sales and the health of the semiconductor industry. Analysts expect third-quarter revenue to rise 23% to $13.12 billion and adjusted profit to increase 39% to $12.05 per share, per Koyfin, with investors focused on equipment orders, demand trends, and the company's outlook.
ASML previously raised its 2026 revenue outlook in July, reflecting continued demand for its lithography systems, and traders will look for indications that this momentum can continue.

TSMC’s Q3 Revenue Surges 50% to Record, Can the Stock Keep Climbing?
sum: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSM), the world’s largest contract chipmaker, posted record third-quarter revenue as surging demand for AI applications continued to power semiconductor sales. Revenue for the July-through-September period reached NT$1.49 trillion ($46.71 billion), up 50% from a year earlier.
The quarter notched a fresh all-time high and exceeded both Wall Street’s and the company’s own targets on multiple fronts.

LSEG SmartEstimate had projected Q3 revenue of NT$1.46 trillion, leaving the actual result about NT$300 billion above consensus. September alone brought in NT$511.86 billion, up 54.6% year over year, though it slipped 0.6% from August.

TSMC’s own Q3 guidance, issued with second-quarter results, had called for revenue of $44.6 billion to $45.8 billion. The $46.71 billion print came in above the top end of that range. At the time, the company also guided for a gross margin of 65%–67% and an operating margin of 56%–58%; the actual figures will be disclosed with the full report.

For the first nine months of 2026, TSMC’s cumulative revenue rose 41.1% year over year to NT$3.90 trillion, underscoring the sustained strength in demand for advanced chips used in AI accelerators and data centers.

TSMC said alongside its second-quarter results that third-quarter business would be underpinned by continued strong demand for leading-edge process technologies, including the ramp-up of its 2-nanometer technology.

For the first three quarters of 2026, TSMC's cumulative consolidated revenue reached approximately NT$3.898727 trillion (approximately $122.1 billion), up 41.1% year-over-year, also the best performance for the same period in the company's history.

At its second-quarter earnings call, TSMC guided third-quarter revenue in US dollar terms to a range of $44.6 billion to $45.8 billion. Based on an assumed exchange rate of NT$32 per US dollar, the corresponding New Taiwan dollar revenue range was approximately NT$1.4272 trillion to NT$1.4656 trillion. With September revenue now reported, the actual third-quarter result has comfortably exceeded the upper end of guidance, outperforming market expectations.
Note: Q3 figures reflect company guidance converted at NT$32 per US dollar; September figures reflect sell-side consensus estimates.

Analysts had originally estimated TSMC's September revenue would land between NT$444.8 billion and NT$483.2 billion, with an average expectation of a roughly 9.9% month-over-month decline. The actual figure of NT$511.857 billion not only beat the consensus estimate but showed a month-over-month decline of just 0.6%, indicating that shipment momentum for advanced process nodes was far stronger than anticipated.

Using the midpoint of the third-quarter guidance in US dollar terms, quarter-over-quarter growth would have been approximately 12% and year-over-year growth approximately 37%. However, the final New Taiwan dollar revenue posted year-over-year growth of 50.94% and quarter-over-quarter growth of 17.62%, with explosive AI-related order momentum serving as the primary engine driving revenue.

sum: Artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure spending isn't slowing down, and that's not surprising, as major hyperscalers and AI companies need to fulfill massive contractual backlogs.

Taiwan Semiconductor Is a No-Brainer Buy On Repeat And Not For The Reason You Think
sum: Everyone buying TSMC stock is watching the wrong number. The real reason to own shares hides one layer beneath the AI headlines, inside a bottleneck so tight that even TSMC's own customers cannot get enough of it.

I keep adding shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM | TSM Price Prediction), and the reason has almost nothing to do with the AI accelerator headlines you have been reading. The reason lives one layer deeper, inside a packaging technology called Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate. The market routinely focuses on TSMC’s nanometer logic nodes (3nm, 2nm, A16), but the real choke point in modern AI accelerators is advanced packaging, specifically CoWoS. Once I understood that, my conviction stopped wavering.

Management put it plainly on the Q2 call: “Our packaging capacity is so tight that now it’s a little bit of my customers’ growth.” That is a foundry telling you demand exceeds what it can physically ship, and the constraint sits in the substrate and interposer step between the die and the board, not in the transistors themselves. Every leading AI accelerator on the market flows through this bottleneck, and TSMC owns it.

The financials confirm the pricing power that comes with a chokepoint. In Q2 2026, TSMC posted EPS of $4.31 against a $3.8866 estimate, a 10.89% beat, on revenue of $40.2 billion, up 36.0% year over year. Gross margin came in at 67.7%, up 9.1 percentage points year over year. Advanced nodes at 7nm and below made up 77% of wafer revenue, with 3nm at 30%, 5nm at 33%, and 2nm debuting at 3% in its first commercial quarter. Then August monthly revenue landed up 53.3% year over year, and management raised full-year 2026 growth guidance to “slightly above 40% year-over-year in U.S. dollar terms.”

The obvious alternatives get reached for first, and I have passed on each. Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) is an integrated device maker that has repeatedly missed on leading-edge execution while TSMC ships 305 distinct process technologies and debuted A13 at the 2026 North America Technology Symposium. GlobalFoundries (NASDAQ:GFS) is a trailing-edge foundry with no sub-7nm exposure, meaning it does not compete for the wafer mix that generated 77% of TSMC’s revenue.

sum: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM -2.15%) has been one of the top artificial intelligence (AI) stocks to own. TSMC holds a unique position in the chipmaking world, and that dominance has allowed the company to reach new heights.

However, I think it's far from done setting all-time highs, and it could reach levels never before seen by the time 2027 rolls around. I think it could get all the way up to $600 per share fairly easily by the end of next year, making it a no-brainer stock to buy right now.

TSMC is the only reason AI technology is where it is now. It's a chip foundry, which means clients come to it with chip designs, and it manufactures them. This is a great place to be, as it allows the company to stay neutral in the AI race and fabricate chips for competing companies (such as Nvidia and AMD). However, TSMC also has a unique position in terms of size.

During 2025, research by The Motley Fool found that TSMC accounted for over 70% of chip foundry revenue in the world. That means that if one of the major AI firms wanted to switch to a different chip foundry, it probably wouldn't have enough production capacity to meet demand. The sheer size of TSMC versus its competition gives it a major competitive advantage, and it allows investors to easily project how TSMC will grow over the next few years, as it's likely to grow in lockstep with AI spending increases.

Next year, Wall Street analysts expect the company's revenue to rise 34% year over year. That suggests another fantastic year for the company, and with TSMC trading at a reasonable valuation, I think it could be in for major stock price growth.
TSMC tends to trade at around 28 times forward earnings as the year ends. Currently, the company trades at about 20 times next year's earnings.

If TSMC can rise to 28 times forward earnings by the end of 2027, there's about 41% upside in TSMC's stock. At today's $435 price tag, that indicates a $612 stock price by the end of next year. That's great upside in one year, and given Wall Street analysts' history of underestimating TSMC's growth during the AI build-out, its true potential could be far higher.

sum: The TAIEX (Taiwan Stock Exchange Capitalization Weighted Stock Index) is the main benchmark for stocks listed on the Taiwan Stock Exchange. Market-cap weighted and dominated by semiconductor and technology companies, it has been one of the strongest major equity indices over the past twelve months, rising more than 70% at its peak on the back of the global AI boom.

That momentum has now broken. After hitting an all-time high above 48,000 in late June, the index has sold off sharply. On 29 July it closed at 40,039, extending a multi-session decline that echoes the recent collapse in South Korea’s KOSPI.

TSMC, Taiwan’s dominant company, accounts for more than 40% of the TAIEX. Listed on both the Taiwan Stock Exchange and the New York Stock Exchange, it had largely shrugged off earlier turbulence in the wider AI sector.

In July so far TSMC has dropped more than 17 percent since its June high of $477. Nvidia, Broadcom, and others have performed better. This may come as a surprise to some following on from TSMC’s recent results on July 16.

The firm’s second quarter net profit rose 77 percent year-on-year, marking its ninth straight quarter of double-digit growth. TSMC even raised its full-year 2026 revenue growth outlook to above 40 percent from above 30 percent.
Not only that, but the firm has also announced investing another $100 billion to expand its chipmaking in Arizona. This takes combined spending plans in the U.S. to $265 billion.
Despite the strong results and expansion plans, the share price has continued to fall. Several factors have converged.

sum: Taiwan's stock market staged a dramatic performance today (July 29). Under pressure from consecutive sharp declines in the U.S. Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, the Taiwan Weighted Index briefly turned positive in early trading before selling pressure cascaded, sending the index plunging more than 1,000 points at one stage. It breached the 41,000-point threshold, hitting an intraday low of 40,546 points, before bargain-hunting buyers stepped in, significantly narrowing the decline to around 500 points as the index seesawed fiercely near the 41,000 level.

Taiwan's "national champion" TSMC (2330.TW) became the main battleground for bulls and bears today. The stock opened lower and then tumbled NT$30 to hit NT$2,250, with its market capitalization fluctuating wildly. Looking back at the previous trading session, TSMC had already been hit by a double whammy: the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell more than 2% and Nvidia plunged 5%. TSMC's share price gapped down in early trading, dropping as much as 3.4% intraday to NT$2,270, wiping out more than NT$2 trillion in market value.

This wave of selling pressure is not unique to Taiwan's market. According to a Bloomberg report on July 28, the Bloomberg Asia Pacific Semiconductor Index, which tracks Asian chip stocks, fell as much as 7.5% that day, marking its largest single-day drop since March of this year. South Korea's Kospi index tumbled nearly 11%, with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix both plunging more than 13%. Japan's Nikkei 225 and Taiwan's Weighted Index both fell about 4%. The U.S. Nasdaq 100 Index dropped 1.8% on the same day, falling more than 10% from its historical high and officially entering correction territory. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) had already declined for a fourth consecutive session, its longest losing streak this year.

At its root, this global chip stock sell-off was triggered by two intertwined factors. First, a Reuters exclusive report on July 28 revealed that Chinese state-owned enterprise Shanghai Jisena Electronic Technology Group has begun mass production of immersion deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography machines, with plans to ship about 5 units this year and increase to approximately 20 units by 2027.

Media giant Comcast saw its stock price surge over 10% during the session, marking its largest single-day gain since 2020. Market reports indicated the company plans to spin off its NBCUniversal business, a structural restructuring plan that received strong investor approval, triggering a massive influx of capital.

Chinese ADRs performed relatively strongly, with the Nasdaq Golden Dragon Index rising nearly 2%. Among them, UP Fintech surged nearly 8%, while Baidu, Full Truck Alliance, and Miniso all gained over 5%. NetEase, Youdao, Kingsoft Cloud, and Pony.ai also rose about 4%, forming another bullish force on the day's board.
